'''Orlando Lamar Pace''' (born November 4, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[offensive tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 13 seasons, primarily with the [[St. Louis Rams]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]], winning the [[Lombardi Award]] in 1995 after blocking for [[Eddie George]] during his [[Heisman Trophy|Heisman]] campaign. The following season, Pace won the [[Outland Trophy]], his second Lombardi Award, the [[Touchdown Club of Columbus#Jim Parker Trophy|Jim Parker Trophy]], and [[UPI Lineman of the Year (College)|UPI Lineman of the Year]]. Pace was selected [[list of first overall NFL draft picks|first overall]] in the [[1997 NFL draft]] by the Rams, where he spent all but one season of his professional career. This included being a member of the [[The Greatest Show on Turf|Greatest Show on Turf]]. In his final season, he was a member of the [[Chicago Bears]].

With the Rams, Pace was recognized as the cornerstone of an offensive line that blocked for an offense with the most gross yardage, second-highest completion percentage, and fifth-most touchdown passes during his 12 years with the team. Under Pace's protection, the Rams passing offense compiled more than 3,000 yards per season in each of the years he played, seven different quarterbacks eclipsed 3,000 yards in a season, and seven players rushed for 1,000 yards. Pace also protected the league's [[National Football League Most Valuable Player Award|Most Valuable Player]] (MVP) recipient for three consecutive seasons, blocking for 1999 and 2001 MVP [[Kurt Warner]] and 2000 MVP [[Marshall Faulk]].

Retiring as a seven-time [[Pro Bowl]] and three-time first-team [[All-Pro]] selection, Pace was a core contributor of the Rams [[The Greatest Show on Turf|Greatest Show on Turf]] offense that won the franchise's first [[Super Bowl]] title in [[Super Bowl XXXIV]]. He was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2013 and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2016.

'''Orlando Bernardo Ruff''' (born September 28, 1976, in [[Charleston, South Carolina]]) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[San Diego Chargers]], [[New Orleans Saints]] and [[Cleveland Browns]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Furman Paladins football|Furman Paladins]], departing as the fourth ranking player in school history with 488 career tackles.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Newton |first1=David |title=Next Stop: The NFL |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-state-next-stop-the-nfl/175882025/ |access-date=4 July 2025 |work=[[The State (newspaper)|The State]] |date=14 April 1999 |location=Columbia, South Carolina |pages=[https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-state-next-stop-the-nfl/175882025/ C1] & [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-state-ruff/175882075/ C8] |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

He was signed in 1999 as an undrafted free agent by the [[San Diego Chargers]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Newton |first1=David |title=A sort of homecoming for Chargers' Ruff |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-state-a-sort-of-homecoming-for-charg/175882198/ |access-date=4 July 2025 |work=[[The State (newspaper)|The State]] |date=17 December 2000 |location=Columbia, South Carolina |page=C9 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> While there, he was named Special Teams Player of the Year in 1999 and 2002), and was stout against the run as a starter during the 2000 and 2001 seasons. He departed in 2003 via free agency.

Ruff subsequently signed in the spring of 2003 with the [[New Orleans Saints]]. He remained there for two seasons as middle linebacker. During his tenure in New Orleans, he finished second in overall tackles for two consecutive years.

He concluded his career in 2005 with the Cleveland Browns.

In his NFL career, Orlando played in 108 games. During that stint he finished with a total of 344 tackles, one sack and three interceptions.

'''Omar Douglas''' (born January 10, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for the [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Minnesota Golden Gophers football|Minnesota Golden Gophers]]. Douglas was signed by the Giants as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 1994. He played for the Giants for 4 seasons and appeared in 18 games.

Douglas scored a late-game touchdown in a 1995 game against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] when he recovered a fumbled punt attempt and ran it 41 yards.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20181118192052/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-859674.html "EAGLES 17, GIANTS 14; Zordich Makes Best Of Bad Day"], ''[[The Washington Post]]'',  October 16, 1995.</ref>  In 1997 he suffered a torn [[anterior cruciate ligament]] during training camp. He returned to the team the following year,<ref>Bill Pennington, [https://www.nytimes.com/1998/08/02/sports/pro-football-the-reality-of-camp-it-must-be-brutal.html "PRO FOOTBALL; The Reality Of Camp: It Must Be Brutal"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', August 2, 1998.</ref> but the Giants released him on August 22, 1998.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20171231211916/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-62565123.html "Birk gets chances all down the line"], ''[[Star Tribune]]'', August 27, 1998.</ref>

Douglas attended the [[University of Minnesota]], where he had 130 receptions for 1,681 yards and 14 touchdowns, and set school records for  season and single game touchdown receptions.   He was also a sprinter for Minnesota and won the [[Big Ten Conference|Big Ten]] indoor 55-meter championship in 1994.<ref>[http://www.gophersports.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/102110aab.html "Classic Re-Write: Omar Douglas"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231212049/http://www.gophersports.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/102110aab.html |date=December 31, 2017 }}, [[University of Minnesota]] (accessed December 31, 2017).</ref>

Douglas attended [[Isidore Newman School]] in [[New Orleans]], and he was the first Newman alumnus to play in the NFL.<ref>Matt Winkeljohn, [http://www.espn.com/college-sports/recruiting/football/news/story?id=5179792 "Manning brothers lift Isidore Newman"], [[ESPN.com]], May 11, 2010.</ref>  After his football career ended, Douglas became a business executive.  His son Demetrius [[National Letter of Intent|signed]] to play football for Minnesota in 2017.<ref>Andy Greder, [https://www.twincities.com/2017/01/14/gophers-football-fleck-flips-legacy-recruit-demetrius-douglas-from-oregon/ "Gophers football: Fleck flips legacy recruit Demetrius Douglas from Oregon"], ''[[Pioneer Press]]'', January 14, 2017.</ref>
